name: Sexual market value (SMV)

lead: Sexual market value (SMV) is slang for how desirable someone is as a sexual or romantic partner, treated as a score in a dating marketplace. In looksmaxxing it is the goal that appearance improvements are said to raise, so users rank skin, hair, fitness and style by how much they might add.

SMV is described as a mix of facial attractiveness, height, body, status and money. Academics do not use the term, but they study related ideas such as sexual or erotic capital, mate value, the pay premium for attractiveness and the matching hypothesis. The community's specific weightings have not been tested.

paras: People use it as a framework for ranking themselves and others, often with decile scales or PSL, then pick the cheapest high-impact changes first, such as grooming, hairstyle, fitness and clothing.

No validated instrument measures SMV, and critics of related academic theories argue they overstate individual ownership of attractiveness and overlook culture, class and race. Community discussion includes race-based tier lists that scholars of sexual racism describe as reflecting bias in dating markets.

angle.text: Manosphere and looksmaxxing users treat SMV as a total desirability score, with looks as one part, and use it to prioritise changes such as skin, hair, fitness and style that they expect to bring more attention from potential partners. It is a community term loosely related to academic mate-value research.

lead: Sexual market value, usually abbreviated SMV, is a term used mainly in manosphere, pick-up artist and looksmaxxing communities for a person's overall desirability as a sexual or romantic partner. It treats dating as a market in which individuals have a comparable value that determines the partners they can attract. [1]

The term is not an established concept in academic psychology. The closest scholarly ideas are 'sexual capital' or 'erotic capital', terms used by sociologists and economists for the social power or resources a person gains from sexual attractiveness, and mate-value and matching research in social psychology. [1][1]

On looksmax.org SMV appears in ratings, 'SMV battle' threads comparing celebrities, and debates about how race, height and facial features affect it. [2][3][4] Looksmaxxing frames its projects, from skincare to surgery, as ways to raise SMV.
infobox: Pick-up artist forums, later manosphere and incel communities
Sexual capital, erotic capital, mate value
1 to 10 decile scale, PSL scale (1 to 8), LMS (looks, money, status)

paras: In community usage, a person's SMV is a rank or score summarizing how attractive they would be to potential partners. Raters commonly use a 1 to 10 decile scale or the 1 to 8 PSL scale, and some use a 'looks, money, status' (LMS) framework in which men with top ranks are called 'Chads' and those at the bottom 'incels'. [1]

Posts on looksmax.org use SMV to describe both individuals and groups, for example in threads ranking celebrities against each other or discussing whether the brain gives a distorted view of one's own SMV. [2][5]

Wikipedia's article on sexual capital says the term SMV originated on pick-up artist forums and spread to incel communities, where it parallels the academic idea of sexual capital. [1] The academic term 'erotic capital' was coined by the British sociologist Catherine Hakim in the early 2000s, building on Pierre Bourdieu's forms of capital. [1]

In economics, Robert T. Michael (2004) extended Gary Becker's human capital theory to 'sexual capital', and sociologist Adam Isaiah Green (2008, 2014) proposed that sexual capital is relative to a 'sexual field' and can be traded for other forms of capital. [1]

Hamermesh and Biddle (1993, 1998) found that attractiveness correlates with higher income even after controlling for other factors, and Hamermesh's later book reviews the economic benefits of looks, which he attributes in part to discrimination. [1]

The matching hypothesis, first proposed by Elaine Hatfield (Walster) and colleagues in 1966, holds that people tend to form committed relationships with partners of similar social desirability, especially physical attractiveness. A summary reports support from studies of couples, but also criticism that matching may reflect fear of rejection rather than a preference for similarity. [6]

Scholars summarized on Wikipedia report that in the United States white men are reported to hold the most sexual capital, that Asian American men's socioeconomic success does not improve their dating prospects (Kao et al., 2018), and that on a gay dating app white, taller and more muscular men receive more attention (Riggs et al., 2017; Callander et al., 2016). [1]

Green argues that no single hegemonic form of sexual capital exists and that currencies vary by social group. Critics of Hakim argue that her theory, though presented as universal, mainly concerns women and ignores variation by culture and class (Boislard et al., 2016), and Green (2013) contends that sexual capital is not a portable personal possession. [1]

No studies found. There are no clinical studies of SMV as defined in community usage. Related academic research on sexual capital, attractiveness pay premiums and the matching hypothesis consists of economic and social-psychological studies, summarized above. [1][6]

SMV functions as the framing for much looksmaxxing: users describe interventions as 'SMV maxxing' and debate which traits matter most. [2] Threads on the forum include celebrity 'SMV battles', race-based SMV tier lists, and discussions of whether the community overestimates how attractive women's partners are. [3][4][7][8]
Some members push back on the framing, with titles such as 'why do ppl on this site think that every woman has an unlimited smv' or posts about the brain distorting perceived SMV. [5][8]
